title: "Get the Girl to Check the Numbers"
text:
Katherine Johnson joined the Langley laboratory of NACA, NASA's predecessor, in 1953 as a "computer": one of the women hired to do complex calculations by hand. She started in the West Area Computing unit, a segregated group of African American women mathematicians, and was soon assigned to the flight research division. She worked on the trajectory for Alan Shepard's flight, the first American in space, in 1961.

By the time John Glenn prepared to become the first American to orbit the Earth, in February 1962, the orbital calculations were being done by NASA's new IBM electronic computers. Glenn was wary of them. According to Johnson's own account, recounted by Margot Lee Shetterly, he asked the engineers to "get the girl to check the numbers," and said that if she confirmed them, he was ready to go.

Johnson worked through the equations herself on a desktop mechanical calculator, following the spacecraft's path through its orbits. It took her about a day and a half. Her figures matched the machine's.

On 20 February 1962 Glenn flew three orbits in Friendship 7 and came home safely. Johnson went on to work on calculations for the Apollo program, and in 2015 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
lesson: Trust in a team comes from proven competence. When the stakes are high, the person you rely on should be the one who has earned it, whoever they are.
location: NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, Virginia, USA
source: NASA oral history interviews with Katherine Johnson; Margot Lee Shetterly, Hidden Figures (2016)
caveat: Glenn's exact words come from later recollections rather than contemporary records.
